title: Notes of Ministry - 86 - January 1980

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 86 - January 19 (2044)/Notes of Ministry - 86 - Januar - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: When the Jews returned from Babylon and built the wall they were in great weakness. It was a small remnant that returned. They were marked by much devotion and a considerable degree of fear and trembling, so much so that in the passage we read earlier they were encouraged that “The joy of Jehovah is your strength”, Nehemiah 8: 10. In these prevalent conditions of weakness they had to look to God Himself for their strength, support, and help.

There is no doubt, beloved brethren, and I do not need to emphasize it in the least, that we live in conditions of weakness at the present time. There is numerical weakness generally, and weakness in the number of our gatherings, and in these circumstances we have to find our strength outside of ourselves. It is one of the lessons that the Lord is teaching His people these days, the blessedness of finding their strength outside of themselves in another source and in another Person altogether.

Man is naturally an independent creature, his whole environment is built up in the sense that he feels able to cope with things himself, only it is very evident if you look at the public scene that he is totally unable to cope with things. There is not a sphere, economically, politically, or in the sense of what is moral, in which man is able to cope. His inability and his weakness are manifest, and what is more solemn is that in that manifest weakness he knows no source outside of himself to turn to; but a believer does. That is the great difference between a person who is in the possession of the Holy Spirit and a person who is not. The former has a source he can turn to outside of himself, a proved source. Oft-times in an emergency men derive passing help from a certain source, and when they resort to it again in another emergency it is unavailing, but not so the believer. No matter what the crisis, the test, or the situation that the believer, or the testimony, is found in, in turning to that source outside of ourselves we find it is still the same, still abundant, still powerful, still free, in supplying what is needed for that moment.

Now I want to turn to these scriptures to show how, in conditions of outward weakness, there was a sense of the power and strength of God, over and above those conditions. I turn to Paul in Corinthians, and while it is largely what we call a levitical experience he relates (it was his experience as a minister entrusted with light from God, having received this great revelation as taken up to the third heaven), there is in it what is of profound help which abides as an instruction and an encouragement to us. Paul says that a thorn for the flesh was given to him and it was not to be taken away, even after three requests that it should be. In that sense, beloved brethren—bear with me in the use of the word—it remained with him governmentally all his life. In other words, there was a circumstance attached to his life that remained. We find that often in our personal histories, that there is something that the Lord has to bring in just to take us out of any self-sufficiency we have in our own strength, and it remains with us. It may be in the disposition of the Lord as to where He places us. It may be in a matter of health, or physical afflictions which, humanly speaking, would impair our efficiency and our enjoyment of divine things. I am sure we have said at least once in our lives in regard to a certain thing, ‘I would have been better without this’, or at least we have said, ‘I perhaps could get on better in another place’. In other words, the flesh has raised a certain resentment in our spirits against an imposition that the Lord has placed upon us in His ways, and in His government.

Now, beloved brethren, the Lord loves us; we know that. He loves us, every one of us. There is not a believer in this room, and let me say there is not a believer anywhere who has trusted His precious blood, but the Lord loves them. Now let us think of that. As we contemplate the loaf on a Lord’s day morning, let us never forget that, the Lord’s love for His own. As knowing that, and as conscious of it, coming down to ourselves, we get that assurance, though we feel so weak at times in the circumstance in which the Lord may place us.

Paul says, “I thrice besought the Lord that it might depart from me”. He besought the Lord thrice, and I think you know the reason the Lord did not remove it. If the Lord had, so to speak, endorsed the thought that Paul would have been a more effective servant without it.

He would have taken it away—but in leaving it, it was to bring out in Paul where the source of his strength lay. It lay not in himself, not in his own power, not in his own ability, and not in his own mind; it lay in grace—“My grace suffices thee”. Has every one of us learned in circumstances of great weakness what the power of grace can do, when circumstances have been overwhelming governmentally? You know, brethren, we are all suffering governmentally today for the history of things. That is a solemn fact. To say that we are suffering governmentally does not necessarily mean that we are the subject of God’s government in regard to sin we have done. What I am saying is that there is a certain governmental position, and we are all suffering from it in the loss of our families, the loss of our brethren, and the general declension of things. How do you carry on?—“My grace suffices thee”. In other words the Lord is telling us, ‘I could give more brethren; I could move miraculously in the healing of things in the divisions that have taken place’. He could do that, but His word to us is, “My grace suffices thee; for my power is perfected in weakness”. Paul says he will rather boast in his weaknesses, “that the power of the Christ may dwell upon me”.

Now there is a difference between “My grace” and “the power of the Christ”. “My grace” is the divine supply that comes into your spirit in meeting the exercise, but “the power of the Christ” is a reference to His priesthood. It is a reference to the place He occupies on high as the Priest, and who has not in times of weakness been thankful for the strengthening power of our Priest? Oh, the priestly service of Christ!—when you felt things so overwhelming, to find the power of the Christ ‘dwelling’. Now that word ‘dwelling’ is ‘tabernacle’. In other words there is a certain state of contentment and restfulness in your links with divine Persons. No matter how weak you are and however testing the circumstance may be, “the power of the Christ”, the power of His priestly service, is available at all times. Some of you, dear brethren, are in very small conditions; perhaps you are the only person in a place. You may feel so weak that you cannot take the step which you feel inwardly you should take and which the Lord is laying upon you. Remember, “My grace suffices thee”, and the power of Christ will rest, upon you.

In 1 Kings 20 we find not so much an individual thought as a collective thought. The whole power of the Syrians was ranged against Israel at that time. The opposition was formidable. It is a reference to the whole world power as arrayed against the testimony of God. The forces of this world are arrayed against all that the people of God seek to hold for Himself. Syria represents that. It says that “the children of Israel were numbered and victualled”. It is a reference to our local meetings. We have had to get down to that, to numbering our local meetings, so that if one is absent our hearts go up—Where is he tonight?’, ‘Where is she tonight?’ In days of weakness every one is valuable.

That old sister who cannot get out to the meetings for the burden of her age and her bodily weakness—Oh, she is valuable, she is numbered, and perhaps her prayers are going to do something to the Syrian host. Her prayers are going to be effective. And it says they were victualled, they were fed. Why does the Lord set responsible men in a locality? He sets them there so that God’s people are fed.

The responsibility of a brother of weight and experience in any meeting is to ensure that the saints are fed. There will be no power to stand against weakness, there will be no power to stand against the enemy, unless they are numbered and victualled. It could have said numbered and fed, but it does not say that. It means that they were supplied with good substantial food. Mr. Taylor used to warn us to beware of novelties. Value the Scriptures; keep them constantly before you, and regulate what is ministered in the light of the Scriptures and in the framework of the ministries that the Lord has given, because while under the Spirit in these days there is what is fresh, in the light of the revelation of God there is nothing new.

We accept that. An old brother in Scotland used to say, ‘If it is new, it is not true; if it is true, it is not new’. Not that what you get is not fresh, but the revelation of God is complete and the ministries of the recovery, the accredited ministries, have brought out its scope for us to explore, so that we get these fresh touches.

Israel were, it says, “like two little flocks of goats; but the Syrians filled the land”. Goats do not normally go in flocks; I have never seen a flock of goats in my life. It is wonderful what christianity can do, wonderful what can be done under the power of grace. Think of that flock of goats at Antioch in Acts 13. Barnabas, Saul, Niger, a coloured man, one out of Herod’s palace, and so on. There they were, that little flock of goats, and their strength lay in the spiritual significance of that word ‘goat’. That is, they understood something of the power of separation being maintained; not separation based on legal precept, but the idea of the goat is that separation comes from holiness and a desire that things might be preserved and maintained for the pleasure of God. There is no power so great in dealing with the Syrian hosts as a little company of people, separate from the world and all that marks it, walking in the light as God is in the light and having fellowship with one another. They can defeat the Syrians. It is so and it will be so, provided we find our strength, our support and our resource in the Spirit.

In Psalm 84 we find what relates more to the privilege side. It says, “How amiable are thy tabernacles, O Jehovah of hosts!”, another link with the thought of the tabernacle. Then, “My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of Jehovah; my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God”. How expressive that is, is it not, of the desires that the Holy Spirit would put in the heart of believers that they long not only for the company of God Himself, known in their individual circumstances, but they long for the company of God in His dwelling, in His own place. Is everybody in this room like that? Does your heart cry out for the living God? Do you long for His tabernacles? Do you long for the gathering of God’s people, where God is served, where His name is cherished? “Thine altars”, it says; why does it refer to the altars? It is a reference to the service of God.

I was speaking just this week to a young man who used to be with us and I said to him, ‘Do you never long for the Lord’s supper?’ Does your heart never long for the Lord’s supper? Here it is—“How amiable are thy tabernacles, O Jehovah ... Blessed are they that dwell in thy house—they will be constantly praising thee” and “Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee—they, in whose heart are the highways”. O, beloved, are the highways in our hearts? If the highways are in your heart you will long for the tabernacles, you will long for the altars, you will long for the dwelling-place of God. If the highways are in your heart you will love them. You will love what is collective. “Blessed ... they, in whose heart are the highways”; it is a reference to the Israelites when they were far away from Jerusalem; as the feast of booths came round they would say, “How amiable are thy tabernacles”. In other words, they were saying, ‘We wish we were there’. In their heart were the highways; they were thinking of the road back, up to Jerusalem, up to Zion, up to the service of God.

Then it says, “Passing through the valley of Baca”, that is, the valley of tears. Sometimes the road up to the feast of booths is a valley, of Baca. Some of us have proved that, many here have proved it, that the road up to the tabernacles is sometimes, oft-times, a valley of Baca. It means weeping, it means testing, it means sorrow, but it says “they make it a well-spring”. Oh, can you make the valley of Baca a well-spring? Can you get the help of the Holy Spirit as you go up that road? As you go up the valley of Baca, and the tears and exercises of it burden you, can you make it a well-spring? Have you power in the Holy Spirit? Can you draw on the resources in the Scriptures? “The early rain covereth it with blessings”. How thankful we are for that! And the valley of Baca has been for many not a wholly desolate place. We have found that the early rain has covered it with blessings. I understand that if you walked along the valley of Baca and you saw a crevice in the road, there would be water in it. Every sorrow brings its own recompense and the comfort that the Lord gives.

It says, “They go from strength to strength”. Now that is not altogether a cumulative thought. It does not mean that you have some strength, then you get some more, and as you move on you get yet more strength. “They go from strength to strength” means that in each step you take in the valley of Baca you get strength for that step. In other words it is to keep you absolutely and perfectly dependent in every step you take. If it were not so, beloved brethren, we would be self-sufficient and say, ‘I am strong enough, I can take the next step because I am strong’; but to go “from strength to strength” means that every step you take along that road, up to the tabernacles of God, you get grace and help and strength for that step. You say, ‘Oh, I can never take that step’. You will get grace for it if you take it. ‘I cannot take the next step’. You take it; you will get grace for it, and the next step, you will get grace for that.

“They go from strength to strength”, and then it says, “each one will appear before God in Zion”. There is no record in Scripture of anybody who lost his way going up to Zion. It says in Isaiah 35: 8 that the way is so simple that even fools shall not err therein. Why? Because you go from strength to strength, and every step you take in dependence on God He will lead you up to the great climax of His house.

Let us be more dependent, brethren. Let us rely more on the Holy Spirit. Let us rely more on the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let us trust God more. Faith is not a blind thing. People speak of ‘blind faith’. There is no such thing. God gives you strength for every step you take, and may all in this room today, some of us feeling very weak in ourselves, prove the strength and help that comes from God for each circumstance, for His name’s sake.

Needless to say, beloved brethren, we have lost a true brother and friend. The apostle John brings forward the thought of the brother early in this gospel; that is the way certain disciples are found. It says of one, “Again, on the morrow, there stood John and two of his disciples”; that was John the Baptist. John said, as he looked at Jesus as He walked, “Behold the Lamb of God”, and hearing the words of John the two disciples followed Jesus (John 1: 37). Our beloved brother was a follower of Jesus. What a privilege to be a follower of Jesus! I trust that every one in this room is, or becomes, a follower of Jesus. There is none other who is great enough to fulfil the desires and the longings of our hearts; we find satisfaction only in Christ.

One of these disciples—Andrew—who left John and followed Jesus, “first finds his own brother Simon ... And he led him to Jesus”. I think our beloved brother would have desired, as we are together today, that we make much of Christ—our Lord Jesus Christ; I know it would have been his earnest desire that everyone here might be led to Jesus. He is the glorious centre, beloved friends and brethren, of God’s universe of bliss. Our beloved brother is asleep through Jesus. The Lord Jesus said of Lazarus, “Lazarus, our friend, is fallen asleep”. Oh the blessedness, and the perfect peace, as one falls asleep through Jesus! It is a peace which this world knows nothing of, but the believer is absolutely secure, in view of rising from the dead to be with Christ for His eternal pleasure.

This chapter brings out that Lazarus was not only a brother, but, as the Lord said, “our friend”. But as we proceed in the chapter one would trust that nothing may eclipse our view of the greatness of Christ. It says, “Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus”.

And the Lord loves us. Martha knew certain terms, as we do, but, like Martha, we may not have a full view. She knew about the resurrection in the last day; she spoke of that—that Lazarus would rise then—but Jesus, in love and tenderness, spoke to her saying, “I am the resurrection and the life”, bringing out the greatness of His Person. The resurrection in the last day will be because He is “the resurrection and the life”.

I refer now to the passage in Revelation. I understand that John, the beloved apostle, was the last writer among the apostles. He wrote this book. His gospel probably was written after this book, for John lived to be a good age. Our brother has had a long, full life. How well and in what detail he has served the beloved brethren! All here would agree to that. We are going to miss him greatly, but the Lord is great enough in His own way to supply what is needed. Yet we feel the loss, and we feel with our beloved sister in her tremendous loss. Who can fathom it? Thank God. Jesus can fathom it! John brings forward the incident of Jesus weeping. He feels with us. Our glorious Saviour and Lord, the blessed Son of God, is able to draw near to our beloved sister and in wondrous grace cause her to lean on His arm, for He will give her the present needed comfort.

This passage in Revelation again brings out the greatness of Christ and of His love—“To him who loves us, and has washed us from our sins in his blood”. This is vital, basic, precious truth—truth which sets us free; the glorious Son Himself can set us free as no other can, and we shall be really free. If we are open for it we can be set wholly free, to know and feel the warmth of His blessed love. It is “Him who loves us, and has washed us from our sins in his blood”. Think of His precious blood being shed; think of Him being the blessed Substitute provided of God for us! There on Calvary’s cross He, the One who knew not sin, was made sin for us in order that we may know what it is to be truly free. These are blessed realities contained within the banks of the rivers of Scripture, the word of God, and they are for our blessing, salvation, and joy at the present time and for all eternity.

Then it says, “And made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father: to him be the glory and the might to the ages of ages. Amen”. It is to Him! Then, “I am the Alpha and the Omega, saith the Lord God, he who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty”. Oh may the simple yet profound word of God comfort us, beloved brethren and friends, as we are together at this time. John displays the spirit of Jesus as he writes; I believe it was the spirit of Jesus that marked off our brother during his pathway here. It was a pathway full of service. I knew our beloved brother for many years, being close to him, and I know that he never sought to put himself forward; he was content to remain hidden, and yet the faithful service that he rendered to his Lord and Master, to his brethren and many another, is well known. He was somewhat like John, the writer of this book, who had every right to refer to himself as an apostle, but preferred to say, “I John, your brother and fellow-partaker in the tribulation and kingdom and patience, in Jesus”.

One would just leave these few words with you, beloved brethren, desiring that, in answer to the many prayers that went up from our brother, what has been said may serve to further the work of God in each one of us, that there may be increased fruit to God, for His name’s sake.

I feel hesitant about speaking because I know there must be a number of brethren here who would appreciate the privilege of saying a word at this time. Our brother has been so well known and so much appreciated that it would be a joy to many to take part. But I feel pressed to call attention to these two passages of Scripture, the first being the statement of the apostle Paul, that he was not ashamed of the glad tidings.

That, I feel, is a very appropriate thing to mention at this time, for our brother was not ashamed of the glad tidings and he spoke about the Lord Jesus to those with whom he worked, to those whom he met, and to those whom he knew well. He ever was ready to speak a word in the power which the Holy Spirit afforded, so that his speaking had an effect upon those to whom he spoke. He had concern regarding his household, too, desiring for them the greatest blessing. May the desires which were in our brother’s heart for them be answered in the grace and wisdom of God! And so I say again, our brother was not ashamed to speak a word in season, and now God is not ashamed to be called his God.

I refer now to the passage in Hebrews. It is very interesting that often it was after persons died that God said that He was their God. When He appeared to Moses in the burning bush, in Exodus 3, He said, “I am ... the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3: 6). They all had died, but God was their God—not simply in memory, but in actuality, for though they had died, they still lived to God! The Lord Jesus tells us that, when He was challenged by the Sadducees as to the resurrection. They tried to prove that resurrection is not workable. Many in the world today resort to such tactics to ease their consciences, but the Lord Jesus said to them, “Ye err, not knowing the scriptures nor the power of God ... But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have ye not read what was spoken to you by God, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not God of the dead, but of the living”, Matthew 22: 29–33. These are the words of Jesus; they give us assurance, so we know that, as Paul said, to depart and be with Christ is “very much better”. Our brother was not ashamed to speak of the glad tidings, to speak well of the Lord Jesus, to speak of the rights of God; and now God is not ashamed to be identified as his God. This should be an encouragement to us to be more faithful and devotedly committed to the path of the will of God. May it indeed be so.

articles.title: OCCUPATION WITH CHRIST
articles.author: P. L. Druckenmiller
articles.place: Words at the burial of Mr, H. C. Midgley, Brooklyn, N.Y.

paragraphs.text: I would like to speak of the Lord Jesus in relation to our brother’s pathway and his life. As has already been said, he would have loved to have attention drawn to the Person of our Lord Jesus Christ at such an occasion. But in doing so it is right to draw attention to the practical fruit of the expression of Christ in the life of our brother and in the life of any person. So on an occasion like this the object really is to set forth the blessedness of a believer’s having departed to be with Christ and the blessedness of the Lord Jesus Himself.
I wish to draw attention to the spirit of Christ in our brother who served some of us in regard to our own recovery. As having the spirit of Christ he knew when to act and when not to act.

I do not desire to be unduly personal, but there was a time when division came in, and I, for one, and a good many others, did not act in the spirit of Christ. I wrote a letter to our beloved brother; he knew it was done in a wrong spirit and he did not answer me. Later, when he had heard that the Lord had brought trouble into my life, he contacted me because he knew that the Lord was working and that that was the time to follow through.

These scriptures have been read because our dear brother set forth the truth of a delivered man whose body had been offered as a living sacrifice. Psalm 16 refers in a beautiful way to Christ. The Spirit of God in writing Scripture, and using David, looked forward to the spirit of Christ expressed in His life and in His death. So verse 10 especially has in mind His death, “neither wilt thou allow thy Holy One to see corruption”. The precious body of the Lord Jesus Christ in death could not see corruption. We know that we have to bury our dead out of our sight because of corruption, but we do that in view of the resurrection. The Lord Jesus did not see corruption; His body was perfect; it was raised in glory—glorious Saviour! And in His work He established the basis for our forgiveness and deliverance.

The scripture referred to earlier (Revelation 1: 5) tells us about our being washed from our sins in His blood, bringing with it the assurance of salvation. I have in mind to emphasize the difference between forgiveness and deliverance, the work of Christ having effected the basis of our obtaining both. If we were in the enjoyment of deliverance we would all be together, all be desirous of saying the same thing. There would not be the need of having to reassure ourselves that we have the forgiveness of sins, and that we are going to be with Jesus should we die, if we took, by the Spirit’s power, the next step of faith which involves personal experience of deliverance out of this body of death while we are still alive. This applies in the sense that the law of sin which yet exists in the members of our body is no longer able to dominate.

The Epistle to the Romans is written to christians. It starts with a wonderful view of the Son of God, but soon enters into the degradation that sin has caused in man. You may wonder why in an epistle to christians the writer goes to such pains to show what has happened in the race. He does so because christendom has overlooked God’s feelings about the breakdown.

This epistle sets out in an orderly way the truth of the gospel of the glory of the blessed God so that we might arrive at the truth of the assembly and the worship of God. Our brother’s life truly set this forth, for he was occupied in service, he was consistently present at assembly occasions, and shouldered responsibility in regard to the testimony. He also searched out the truth in connection with ministry and was sensitive as to anything that was not according to Scripture. We need to be like that. We are to base what we say on the Scriptures, but at the same time it is not just the literality of the Scriptures, it is the spirit and import of what is conveyed in Scripture. We refer rightly to many things by way of application, but that must meet the test of Scripture; the application is to be by the Spirit.

Forgiveness and deliverance are the fruits of the great grace of God reaching us through the work of Christ. These things are available to us, available for faith, to be appropriated livingly by the Spirit of God in our souls. Deliverance as we are speaking of it is that I myself have been superseded in myself by Christ. There are many believers who, sad to say, we do not see at the Lord’s supper, with whom we do not have the fulness of joy and communion, who say, ‘Yes, I am occupied with another Man’. But has that Man eclipsed you? Has He replaced you in yourself? Has He by the Spirit so filled your view that you have no other man before you and are enabled to see all things clearly? This is what our dear brother’s life set forth, without pretence, just simply going on in his day-by-day service, having presented his body “a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God”. I commend this to all our hearts.

With regard to our associations of life, I have read in Philippians because it relates to what our brother said as to persons with whom God is pleased. ‘Associations of life’ is how the footnote to Philippians 3: 20 reads. Read these things for yourselves in the precious word of God, and if anything that comes into your soul here today strikes a chord, I would say, ‘Come and see’. Be attracted by what you hear in the word of God and by what you have seen in the life of our dear brother.

Our life is to be devoted to Christ in heaven where He has gone to await the moment when He will come to raise the sleeping saints and to transform those of us who are still here. This scripture in Philippians refers to “our body of humiliation” in which we are here, in which we feel weakness. In relation to this weakness the priesthood of Christ is operating to help us.

We do not have a High Priest for our failures; we have a Priest for our weakness, to help us not to fail. When we fail we have an Advocate with the Father to help us to feel it so that we may judge ourselves. I would desire to take on in some measure what I have seen in our dear brother; I believe we all would. As we do, the Lord Jesus will be more magnified among us. Our brother knew in himself when the lead was going astray. A man who is in the good of deliverance senses it; he waits God’s time and then in his measure he is not afraid to say something about it, because the Lord has passed us through a time when it was not enough to say, ‘Let the Lord do it’. The Lord wants you and me to be faithful, not just to sit around and wait and say, ‘Let the Lord do it’. There are times, certainly, when we have to wait; there is much that we have to wait about. Our dear departed brother waited; he waited in regard to my recovery and the recovery of others close to me, and many another. He followed us up in his prayers and his feelings, and he waited God’s time. But then he acted; he did something.

Our heart goes out to dear christians gathered in connection with the death of our brother; one longs that we could all sit down and eat the Lord’s supper together, and there is a way to it. The way is for you and for me to get near to divine Persons and to live in Their presence. I commend to us further the other reference in Psalm 16, “Thy countenance is fulness of joy; at thy right hand are pleasures for evermore”. Our brother knew what it was to live in the Lord’s presence, privately and in the assembly. As we gather on assembly occasions we experience the joy of the Lord’s presence, and His presence is certainly deliverance for each one of us as we are conscious of the Holy Spirit’s help in our weakness as we continue, and finish, our pilgrim journey.
(Substance of word)

articles.title: “MY GOD”
articles.author: P. W. Hickmott
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Christchurch, N.Z.

paragraphs.text: What struck us, among other things, on Lord’s day was the name of the Father as it would be on the lips of Jesus. That is something to think about, and as we grow in our measure in the knowledge of Christ I think it would mean more to us, what the name Father meant to Him.

He also says “My God”, and that has been drawn attention to by a man of God in those outstanding readings on ‘Divine Names’ (J.T. N.S. Vol.50, p.172). He said it on the cross; we can solemnly contemplate that moment when Jesus said, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”— His God. Our brother has referred to our God; what a message it was—“I ascend to ... my God and your God”, John 20: 17. Paul could speak of “My God”—“My God shall abundantly supply all your need according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” Philippians 4: 19. What that would be on Paul’s lips, his God. Then what would it be for us as we take up the name of the Father, or the name of God—what knowledge of God is there in us? Our concern would be whether we are growing in the knowledge of God. Is there a result from our experiences, particularly recent experiences, so that as any one of us takes these wonderful names on our lips a deepening knowledge is conveyed in them?

Is this knowledge growing with us as any one of us says, ‘Father’? It would not reach to Paul’s knowledge, and obviously it would not reach to the knowledge, so perfect, unique, and distinct, in Jesus, but it is open to us to grow in the knowledge of the Father, and to grow in the knowledge of God. We are only beginning, some of us, to reach into positive things, but Oh how much is open to us—the real, practical, and living knowledge of God, so that as we use these names they mean more and more to us.

I thought of this verse in Revelation 3 in particular; it is Christ’s God—“Him will I make a pillar in the temple of my God”. I could not attempt to say much about it, but would just draw attention to it. It is addressed to the overcomer in Philadelphia. This is open to us, without any pretentious claim to be Philadelphia, to be a pillar in the temple of Christ’s God. “And he shall go no more at all out”; I suppose it looks forward to finality in the Lord’s mind, but something of it can be anticipated and experienced by us. Many of us have surrendered so much that has been right, and gone off in an awful diversion, and the shame of it hardly leaves us, but think of going no more at all out. May we be preserved from any more departures from the truth, but rather would we not love to sense something of what is suggested in these verses? It involves the assembly, the temple of Christ’s God, being made a pillar in it, and not going out any more. Think of Jesus writing on us personally “the name of my God”. What an indelible matter that would be, the Lord’s own hand involved in this, writing on the Philadelphian overcomer the name of His God, “and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem”. It would involve more than we can say, something indelible written by Christ Himself that relates to the truth of the assembly; not any mere academic idea of it that we may think we have attained to, but something the Lord would come in and do personally to an overcomer—“the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down out of heaven, from my God, and my new name”, It is something to think about in connection with this feature of overcoming, that here in this setting we have these three references to “my God”, to Christ’s God.

Well, may we be stimulated as to it, so that rather than being confined and narrowed in the scope of our thinking we may be enlarged as to this immense matter of having to do with Christ, and having to do with His God. May the Lord help us in it, for His name’s sake.
How brightly Thou hast made to shine,
O God, Thy righteousness divine!
Thy rights Thou could’st not justly waive,
But hast Thyself come forth to save!
What glory shines in Jesus’ face,
Declaring all Thy love and grace!
How Thou hast in Thy Son come down
That Thou might’st have us for Thine own!
Thou hast Thy every right maintained,
And in the cross great glory gained,
Hast shone forth as a Saviour God,
At priceless cost, e’en Jesus’ blood!
Thy righteousness shall we display
When glory crowns the coming day,
But grace, our God, has made us bow
And own Thy rights upon us now.
The rays of righteousness divine
Tell more and more that love of Thine.
We love to sing that Jesus died,
That by His blood we’re justified.

TRACING THINGS TO THEIR SOURCE In New Zealand we were taken to see the source of a river in the mountains. A short walk from the road brought us to a narrow path at the bottom of a deep ravine. It led through dense, dank bush, the river flowing swiftly below us.
Then the track ended and there below us was the river’s source—it emerged, a swift, surging torrent from a mountain cave.

It made us reflect on the happy occupation of the believer in tracing things to their source in God. In Revelation 22: 1 the river of water of life, bright as crystal, goes out of the throne of God and of the Lamb. What living grace has flowed out to us, and we thankfully, worshipfully trace it back to God and to Him who suffered that we might enjoy it. In the service of God we have rich impressions of Himself as the glorious Source of all—“Of him, and through him, and for him are all things—to him be glory for ever. Amen”, Romans 11:13-36. The eternal purpose was His; the divine love which underlies all is His, and the wisdom, power, righteousness, grace, and mercy which have been employed in working out the purpose are His and His alone.

Every day, every hour, we receive blessings and mercies which should become, as we trace them to their Source, happy occasions of praise and thanksgiving to God. Every meal is a fresh reminder of a Father’s love and care, and our, thanksgiving engages us afresh with Him. Our measure of health and strength, mercies at work, at school, at home, and on the road, should lead us constantly back in praise to our God and Father. Every thought of Christ, every fresh glimpse of the truth, should not fail to produce a happy, thankful note of praise to Him who graciously gave it.

It is Paul— and Paul a prisoner—who says to the Ephesians, “Giving thanks at all times for all things to him who is God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ”, Ephesians 5: 20. “By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise continually to God”, Hebrews 13: 15.

We must not abandon the position because of fewness of numbers or because of conflict. God would not have the position abandoned. He will support assembly qualities. It is a question of the altar. In the book of Ezra they set up the altar in its place because of fear of the people of the countries. It is not a question of numbers, but of the altar. God would protect the altar.

I admit that saints who have not entered the holiest may have a measure of happiness, but I cannot admit the lesser thing as a substitute for the greater thing. A saint outside the holiest is occupied with the effects of grace upon himself, but however varied and blessed this action may be, it cannot in any degree equal or be similar to what is known inside in the presence of Christ.
